paper_a.title: On Ideal Lattices and Learning with Errors Over Rings

paper_b.title: On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography

metadata.description: Lyubashevsky-Peikert-Regev (paper 301) explicitly extends Regev's original LWE (paper 302) to the algebraic setting of rings of integers in cyclotomic number fields. Every core ingredient of Regev's reduction has a ring analogue: the LWE distribution becomes Ring-LWE over $R_q^\vee$, the GapSVP/SIVP target lifts to ideal-lattice K-SVP/K-SIVP, the worst-case-to-average-case quantum reduction via DGS is replicated with extra ring-theoretic machinery (CRT decomposition, automorphisms, $\mathfrak{q}_i$-LWE hybrids), and the LWE-based PKE becomes a Ring-LWE PKE with $n$-bit ciphertexts. Both papers are PDF-fallback so confidence is moderate where statements differ.

matches.explanation: Both define the LWE/Ring-LWE sample distribution $A_{s,\chi}$ (paper 302) / $A_{s,\psi}$ (paper 301). Paper 302 works in $\mathbb{Z}_p^n \times \mathbb{Z}_p$ with inner product $\langle a,s\rangle$, while paper 301 lifts the same construction to the ring setting $R_q \times \mathbb{T}$ with ring product $a\cdot s/q$ (the secret living in the codifferent $R_q^\vee$). The shape (uniform $a$, secret-dependent linear functional plus error) is identical; the algebraic ambient changes from $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ to a polynomial ring.

Search Ring-LWE ($R$-$\mathrm{LWE}_{q,\Psi}$) is the ring-theoretic counterpart of Regev's search LWE problem: recover the secret from polynomially many samples of the corresponding $A_{s,\cdot}$ distribution. Same problem template, secret moves from $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ to $R_q^\vee$.

Average-case decision Ring-LWE generalizes the decision flavour of LWE used implicitly in Regev (paper 302 only states LWE as a search problem in DP302.1; the decision version appears via the distinguisher chain LP302.19/LP302.20). Match flagged analogous because paper 302 has no separate `definition`-typed decision-LWE node.

Both express the same `find/distinguish the secret from noisy linear samples' problem; ProbP301.1 phrases it at the problem-statement level for Ring-LWE while DP302.1 is the original LWE definition. The ring product $a\cdot s$ replaces the inner product $\langle a,s\rangle$.

The hard worst-case lattice problems used as the target of the reduction. Paper 302 uses GapSVP and SIVP on arbitrary lattices; paper 301 specializes them to ideal lattices in number fields ($K$-SVP, $K$-SIVP). Ideal-lattice variants are a strict subclass of arbitrary lattices, so the reduction in paper 301 is to a (potentially easier) problem — this is the central content of the ring extension.

Both define the smoothing parameter $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda)$ identically as the smallest $r$ with $\rho_{1/r}(\Lambda^*\setminus\{0\}) \le \varepsilon$. Paper 301 cites Micciancio-Regev (external); paper 302 includes it as Definition 2.10 (paper-origin in 302's listing because Regev co-authored the original).

Discrete Gaussian Sampling. Both define $\mathrm{DGS}^\varphi$ identically (given lattice $L$ and $r > \varphi(L)$, output a sample from $D_{L,r}$). Paper 301 uses the ideal-lattice version $K$-DGS, but the problem template is the same; paper 301 cites Regev 2005, i.e. paper 302's preliminary version.

Error-distribution families. Paper 302's $\Psi_\beta$ is a periodic 1-D Gaussian on $\mathbb{T}$; paper 301's $\Psi_{\le\alpha}$ is a multidimensional elliptical-Gaussian family on $K_\mathbb{R}$. Both parametrize the error class admissible to the reduction; the ring variant is naturally elliptical because the canonical embedding is multi-dimensional.

$\Upsilon_\alpha$ (paper 301) is the random non-spherical noise distribution used in the worst-to-average reduction. Its closest counterpart in paper 302 is $\bar\Psi_\alpha$ (the discretized periodic Gaussian); paper 302 does not use a randomized-parameters distribution because in the scalar case there is no rotational ambiguity to randomize over.

Bounded-distance decoding. Paper 302's $\mathrm{CVP}_{L,d}$ with $d < \lambda_1(L)/2$ is the same problem as paper 301's $K$-$\mathrm{BDD}_{I,d}$ on ideal lattices: given a target within distance $d$, recover the unique closest lattice point.

Quotient-mod-$q$ closest-vector problem. Paper 301's $q$-$\mathrm{BDD}_{I,d}$ asks for the BDD solution modulo $qI$; paper 302's $\mathrm{CVP}^{(p)}_{L,d}$ asks for the coefficients modulo $p$ of the closest lattice point. Same trick: solve BDD mod the modulus instead of exactly.

Main theorem statements. Paper 302's Theorem 1.1: efficient algorithm for LWE $\Rightarrow$ efficient quantum $\tilde O(n/\alpha)$-approximation of GapSVP/SIVP on arbitrary lattices. Paper 301's Theorem 3.6: poly-time quantum reduction from $\tilde O(\sqrt n/\alpha)$-SIVP/SVP on ideal lattices to decision Ring-LWE. The ring version achieves a tighter approximation factor ($\sqrt n$ vs $n$) at the cost of restricting to ideal lattices.

Formal main theorem giving the DGS-style worst-case-to-Ring-LWE reduction (paper 301's Theorem 4.1) corresponds to paper 302's Theorem 3.1 (DGS-to-LWE reduction). Both establish: a (Ring-)LWE oracle yields an efficient quantum algorithm sampling from sufficiently wide discrete Gaussians on the lattice / ideal lattice.

Search-to-decision and worst-case-to-average-case reductions. Paper 302's Lemmas 4.1-4.4 give the (relatively short) chain converting search LWE to decision LWE in the scalar case. Paper 301 needs a substantially more elaborate chain (Theorems 5.1-5.3) because the ring structure forces a hybrid argument over the prime ideals $\mathfrak{q}_i$ of $q$, plus automorphism closure and Rényi-divergence transfer. Same goal, fundamentally heavier ring-specific machinery.

The iterative quantum step at the heart of both reductions. Paper 302's Lemma 3.3: given samples from $D_{L,r}$ and an LWE oracle, produce one sample from $D_{L, r\sqrt n/(\alpha p)}$. Paper 301's Lemma 4.2 is the ring version: given samples from $D_{I,r}$ and a Ring-LWE oracle, produce a sample from $D_{I,r'}$. Both are Regev-style and quantum; paper 301's lemma is slightly stated in the cleaner ring form.

Classical BDD-to-LWE part of the iterative step. Paper 301's Lemma 4.3: classical reduction from BDD on $I^\vee$ to Ring-LWE. Paper 302's Lemmas 3.4 and 3.11: classical reductions from $\mathrm{CVP}_{L^*,d}$ (or its mod-$p$ variant) to LWE using DGS samples. Same classical half of the Regev iterative step, lifted to ideals.

Quantum BDD-to-DGS step. Paper 301 cites Regev 2005 Lemma 3.14 (LP301.13 is `external'); paper 302 contains exactly that lemma as Lemma 3.14 (LP302.15). Same quantum-Fourier-transform argument that turns a CVP/BDD oracle into a discrete Gaussian sampler.

Mod-$q$ suffices for BDD. Paper 301's LP301.14 (`BDD reduces to $q$-BDD', cited from Regev 2005 Lemma 3.5) corresponds to paper 302's Lemma 3.5 (LP302.10): coefficients-mod-$p$ of the closest vector are enough to solve full CVP.

`Continuous-noise smoothing': sampling a discrete Gaussian then adding a continuous Gaussian gives a wider continuous Gaussian. Paper 301's LP301.4 (cited from Regev 2005) is exactly Claim 3.9 / Corollary 3.10 in paper 302.

Smoothing-parameter bounds and the smoothing-implies-near-uniformity lemma. Paper 301 packages these as cited results from Micciancio-Regev/Regev 2005; paper 302 (being one of those originals) contains them as Lemmas 2.11, 2.12 and Claim 3.8.
Banaszczyk's discrete-Gaussian tail bound: a $D_{\Lambda,r}$ sample has norm $> r\sqrt n$ with probability at most $2^{-2n}$. Both papers cite Banaszczyk 1993 Lemma 1.5(i).

The Regev-style iterative quantum dimension-reduction algorithm. Paper 302's AP302.1 (DGS via iterative step) is the canonical algorithm; paper 301's AP301.2 is its ideal-lattice port. Both bootstrap to a very wide Gaussian and apply the iterative step $O(n)$ times, contracting the width geometrically by $\alpha p/\sqrt n$ (or its ring analogue).

BDD-to-LWE reduction algorithm (the classical half of the iterative step). Both papers expose this as a standalone routine: take BDD instance plus DGS samples, output (Ring-)LWE samples whose secret encodes the BDD solution. Paper 301 wraps the construction with a clearing-element $\theta_t$ map (PSP301.1-3) absent in 302; the inner step DAGs differ but the conceptual routine is the same.

Composite L2-vs-L2 mapping for the BDD-to-LWE step decomposition. Paper 302 (PSP302.6-9, inside PP302.3 proving Lemma 3.11) decomposes into: marginal-$a$-uniform, linear-equation form, noise-bound, recover-$s$. Paper 301 (PSP301.1-3) decomposes into: pick clearing element $t$, build LWE samples from DGS, recover BDD solution. Both reach the same conclusion but paper 301 has the extra ring-theoretic step of choosing $t \in I$ coprime to $\langle q\rangle$.

LWE-based public-key cryptosystem. Paper 302's AP302.3 is the original Regev cryptosystem with ciphertext size $O(n)$ and per-bit encryption. Paper 301's AP301.3 is the Ring-LWE PKE described in the introduction: ciphertext is a single pair $(u,v)\in R_q^2$ encrypting an $n$-bit plaintext at once. Same security template (CPA from indistinguishability of $A_{s,\chi}$ from uniform), more compact via ring structure. Paper 302's correctness/security lemmas LP302.23, LP302.24 are absorbed implicitly into AP301.3.

Multiplicative Gaussian smoothing (paper 301 LP301.16): when multiplying a discrete Gaussian by a fixed ring element and adding a continuous Gaussian, the result is again a (now elliptical) Gaussian. Paper 302's Claim 3.9 is the additive scalar version of the same smoothing/convolution principle. Paper 301 needed a multiplicative variant because the ring product replaces the inner product.

$\mathfrak{q}_i$-LWE, hybrid distribution $A^i_{s,\psi}$, and worst-case/average-case decision-LWE relative to a prime $\mathfrak{q}_i$ are paper-301-specific machinery. They have no counterpart in paper 302 because $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has no analogous prime decomposition to exploit; this is the technical novelty of the ring extension.

The full hybrid-over-$\mathfrak{q}_i$ search-to-decision and worst-to-average chain (Lemmas 5.5-5.16). Paper 302 collapses this to a four-lemma chain LP302.19-LP302.22; paper 301's expansion is paper-specific because of the ring prime decomposition and the need for automorphism transitivity.

Algebraic-number-theory infrastructure: ideal-lattice minimum-distance bounds, CRT for $\mathcal{O}_K$, CRT-basis algorithm, clearing-element existence, clearing-the-ideal isomorphism, automorphism transitivity on $\mathfrak{q}_i$. Paper 302 has no need for any of this because it works over $\mathbb{Z}^n$.

Correctness lemma showing the BDD-to-LWE samples constructed via $\theta_t$ have the required ring-LWE distribution (paper 301 Lemma 4.7). The corresponding correctness check in paper 302 is folded into proof PP302.3 / PSP302.6-8 rather than stated as a separate lemma; treated as paper-specific to 301.
The generalized extended Euclidean / CRT-basis algorithm for ring of integers is unique to paper 301; paper 302 has no algebraic-number-theoretic computational primitives.

Rényi-divergence transfer claims used in paper 301's worst-to-average step; paper 302's analogous transfer is a simpler statistical-distance argument (LP302.19, ClP302.2) and does not need Rényi divergence.

Paper-301-specific proofs (Lemmas 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 5.5, 5.9, 5.12, 5.16, Theorems 5.1-5.2). Their conclusions correspond to paper-302 statements (matched at the L1 level above), but the proofs themselves are ring-extended. We do not emit individual proof matches here because the L1 statements they prove are already aligned.

Bootstrapping lemma (Lemma 3.2 of paper 302) producing a very wide DGS sample is used implicitly inside paper 301's iterative algorithm AP301.2 (`initial wide-Gaussian samples $D_{I,r}$ with $r \ge 2^{2n}\lambda_n(I)$') but not stated as a separate lemma in the extracted graph for paper 301.

GIVP-from-DGS and GapCVP$'$-from-DGS reductions (paper 302 Section 3.3). Paper 301's main theorem reduces directly from K-SVP/K-SIVP on ideal lattices to Ring-LWE without going through this intermediate translation, so the corresponding reductions are not separately exposed in 301's graph.

Verifying-LWE-solutions and unknown-$\beta$ lemmas (paper 302 Lemmas 3.6-3.7). Used inside paper 302's classical part of the iterative step; paper 301's analogous machinery (Lemma 4.7 / LP301.15) folds these checks into a single statement.

Banaszczyk transference, Gaussian mass scaling, Poisson summation, local stability of $\rho_s$, smoothing-parameter lower bound, quantum-state approximation claims, and discrete-quantum-Gaussian construction. These are technical lattice/quantum lemmas used inside paper 302's proofs; paper 301 invokes the same underlying facts but cites them by reference rather than restating, so no graph counterpart exists. Confidence low because some are arguably implicit in 301's external citations.

Remarks (`Why quantum?', Peikert classical follow-up) and open problems (dequantization, LPN $p=2$). These are exposition/forward-looking nodes specific to paper 302; remark/open-problem types are auxiliary. (Per compactness rules these wouldn't strictly need `none' entries; we list them here for completeness since they motivate the line of work paper 301 follows.)
